title: Researchers surveyed ancient Arabian desert, finding evidence of lakes but no early human tools
description: Recent studies indicate that early inhabitants of the Arabian Peninsula placed significant importance on freshwater sources and specific types of stones. Researchers extensively examined the vast Rub' al Khali sand sea for archaeological traces. While they discovered remnants of ancient lakes, the absence of stone tools pointed to limited human settlement.

title: How the fossil fuel industry intervenes at COP conferences and in Switzerland
description: Participation by the fossil fuel industry in United Nations climate conferences, including COP31 in Turkey, has drawn criticism. In Switzerland, too, the petroleum sector has sought to downplay its impact on climate change. “If someone tries to burn down your house, you don’t keep inviting them to dinner,” says Elvis Méndez, executive director of the NGO Corporate Accountability. The US-based organisation is calling for restrictions on fossil fuel lobbyists’ access to UN climate conferences, including COP31, which will take place from November 9-20 in Antalya, Turkey. Environmental groups have long criticised the fossil fuel industry’s presence at climate negotiations. While recognising that the industry has a role to play in the energy transition, they argue that its influence on climate policy has helped slow action against global warming. “We have known for decades that burning fossil fuels is the main cause of climate change. title: Europe Ancient Forests Were Open Woodlands, Study Finds
description: A 20-million-year study finds Europe was long a mosaic of open woodlands and meadows, challenging dense-forest reforestation plans.

title: Ancient Maya cities used red pigment in temples; study finds it left mercury in lakes for centuries
description: Ancient Maya civilization used a red pigment made of mercury-rich cinnabar for decoration and rituals. This practice led to significant mercury contamination of nearby lakes and ecosystems. Research indicates that rising mercury levels impacted aquatic organisms and may have affected human health. Previous studies have also shown similar contamination at various Maya sites, raising concerns about widespread environmental impact.
